state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you have a basket of apples, each with a different weight. If you cut all the apples in half, would the heaviest apple still be the heaviest? Think about how changing the values by the same proportion can affect the range in this scenario.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying about the apples. If I cut them in half, the heaviest apple would still be the heaviest, so the range might stay the same. But what about when Katie says if all the plants grow by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \)? Wouldn't that change the range too? I'm still a bit confused about how that works.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it like this: imagine you have a group of friends, each with a different height. If they all grew by the same amount, would the tallest friend still be the tallest? Consider how changing the values by a constant amount affects the range in this situation.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher's apple analogy in Turn 1 is mathematically incorrect (cutting in half does change the range), reinforcing rather than correcting the misconception, and by Turn 2 the student shows increased confusion about both scenarios.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (basket of apples with different weights, group of friends with different heights) to help the student understand abstract mathematical concepts about range and transformations, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
